prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Officials are searching for the driver of a white truck seen on Santiago Canyon Road on Sunday, near the time the Santiago fire started, Orange County authorities said Friday. Chief Chip Prather holds a photo of a white truck similar to the one seen on Santiago Canyon Road. "These people are not suspects at this time," Orange County Fire Authority Chief Chip Prather said. "They are persons of interest who were seen near the fire in a vehicle like this." The vehicle is a white, 1998 to 2004 Ford F150 pickup with chrome tubular running boards. Prather said the information came from a lead called into the investigation's tip line. A $250,000 reward has been offered for information leading to the arrest of the person or persons responsible for the blaze.  Watch how residents feel about arsonist » . The Santiago fire, now 27,000 acres and still burning, was deliberately set, officials said Thursday. Several mandatory evacuations remain in place for the Santiago fire, which has destroyed 14 homes and various other structures. Late Friday afternoon, the blaze moved into Silverado Canyon, authorities said. Sheriff's deputies were evacuating residents in the fire's path.  Watch the Santiago flames rage » . Authorities also suspect arson in the Rosa fire in San Diego County, which burned more than 400 acres before being fully contained. There was no information on the investigation. Elsewhere, the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office filed arson charges Friday against a 41-year-old Sun Valley man who witnesses said set a fire in the West Hills neighborhood and walked away. Catalino Pineda is one of five people who have been arrested in arson investigations this week, but none of them has been linked to the major wildfires raging across Southern California. Pineda was arrested Wednesday after witnesses said they saw him lighting a fire on a hillside, police said. The fire was quickly extinguished. The witnesses followed Pineda to a nearby restaurant and called police, who arrested him. Pineda was expected to be arraigned in Van Nuys Superior Court Friday, Deputy District Attorney Steven Frankland said. He is charged with one count of arson of a structure or forest. Pineda is being held on $75,000 bail and faces up to six years in prison if convicted. In San Bernardino, east of Los Angeles, John Rund, of Hesperia, was arrested Wednesday on arson charges after a witness reported seeing him in brush near the starting point of a fire Tuesday, the sheriff's department said. That fire was quickly put out by passers-by. Investigators are trying to determine if Rund, 48, may have ties to other wildfires. He is being held on $750,000 bail. The San Bernardino County District Attorney's Office on Thursday filed arson charges against Anthony Riperti, 47, of Redlands. A statement from the office did not say when or where Riperti is accused of setting a fire. He is being held on $250,000 bail. In San Diego County, the sheriff's department this week arrested an adult and a juvenile allegedly seen by an anonymous tipster starting a fire in Vista in the northern part of the county. In a written statement, the sheriff's department identified the adult as Gorgonio Nava. The Vista fire Department extinguished the blaze before it grew out of control, the statement said. Investigators have determined that the Grass Valley fire in San Bernardino County was not caused by arson, and a preliminary investigation into the cause of the 11,675-acre Slide fire seems to indicate arson was not a factor, sheriff's spokeswoman Cindy Beaver said. More than 1,600 homes have been destroyed in the past week by Southern California wildfires. E-mail to a friend .

Orange County Fire Authority Chief Chip Prather displayed an image of a truck resembling the vehicle witnesses reported seeing. He emphasized that the occupants were not currently considered suspects, but were people investigators wanted to speak with because they were near the fire in a similar vehicle.

The pickup was described as a white Ford F-150 manufactured between 1998 and 2004 and equipped with chrome tubular running boards. According to Prather, the description came from a tip submitted through the investigation’s telephone tip line.

Authorities have announced a $250,000 reward for information resulting in the arrest of whoever started the fire. Residents have expressed their feelings about the suspected arsonist.

Officials said Thursday that the Santiago blaze had been intentionally ignited. The still-active fire had burned 27,000 acres, destroyed 14 houses and several other buildings, and prompted continuing mandatory evacuation orders. By late Friday afternoon, it had advanced into Silverado Canyon, where sheriff’s deputies were moving people out of threatened areas as the flames continued to spread.

Investigators also believe the Rosa fire in San Diego County may have been deliberately set. That blaze scorched more than 400 acres before crews fully contained it, but authorities released no details about the inquiry.

In a separate case, the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office filed an arson charge Friday against Catalino Pineda, a 41-year-old Sun Valley resident. Witnesses said he started a fire in the West Hills area and then left the scene.

Pineda was among five individuals arrested during arson investigations that week, although none had been connected to the large wildfires burning throughout Southern California. Police said witnesses saw him ignite a hillside fire Wednesday. The flames were extinguished quickly, and the witnesses followed him to a nearby restaurant before contacting officers, who took him into custody.

Deputy District Attorney Steven Frankland said Pineda was scheduled to appear Friday in Van Nuys Superior Court for arraignment. He faced one charge of setting fire to a structure or forest, was held on $75,000 bail, and could receive a prison sentence of up to six years if convicted.

Farther east, in San Bernardino, authorities arrested 48-year-old Hesperia resident John Rund on Wednesday on suspicion of arson. The sheriff’s department said a witness had reported seeing him in brush close to where a fire started Tuesday. People passing by extinguished that blaze before it could spread. Investigators were examining whether Rund might be associated with any other wildfires. His bail was set at $750,000.

The San Bernardino County District Attorney’s Office filed arson charges Thursday against Anthony Riperti, 47, of Redlands. Its statement did not specify when or where he allegedly started a fire. Riperti remained jailed in lieu of $250,000 bail.

In northern San Diego County, sheriff’s deputies arrested an adult and a minor during the week after an anonymous caller allegedly saw them starting a fire in Vista. A written statement from the department identified the adult as Gorgonio Nava. According to that statement, the Vista Fire Department put out the flames before they could become uncontrollable.

Meanwhile, investigators concluded that arson did not cause San Bernardino County’s Grass Valley fire. Sheriff’s spokeswoman Cindy Beaver also said an initial inquiry into the 11,675-acre Slide fire suggested that it, too, was probably not the result of arson.

Wildfires across Southern California had destroyed more than 1,600 homes during the previous week.

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a detailed news report covering the Santiago fire investigation, the $250,000 reward, and the various arson arrests across Southern California.
counterfactuals.output:
**SANTIAGO CANYON, Calif. —** Investigators probing the destructive Santiago Fire in Orange County concluded that the blaze was deliberately set, prompting a multiagency manhunt and a reward that eventually reached **$250,000**. At the same time, law-enforcement agencies across Southern California made several arrests in unrelated arson cases as the region struggled through one of its most severe wildfire outbreaks.

### Santiago Fire treated as a criminal case

The Santiago Fire began on the evening of **October 21, 2007**, near Santiago Canyon and Silverado Canyon in eastern Orange County. Driven by powerful Santa Ana winds, the flames spread rapidly through dry brush, threatened canyon communities and forced thousands of residents to evacuate.

The fire ultimately burned roughly **28,000 acres**, destroyed or damaged homes and outbuildings, and injured several firefighters. It took crews days to bring the perimeter under control, with steep terrain, low humidity and shifting winds complicating suppression efforts.

Investigators said evidence at the origin indicated that the fire had been intentionally ignited. Reports that there were separate points of origin strengthened the determination that the blaze was arson rather than the result of an accident, utility failure or natural cause.

The investigation brought together the Orange County Sheriff’s Department, Orange County Fire Authority and state and federal agencies. Detectives canvassed the canyon, interviewed residents and motorists, examined debris from the suspected ignition area and sought photographs or video recorded near the time the fire began.

Authorities also appealed for information about suspicious people or vehicles seen along canyon roads. Tips were evaluated against witness accounts, dispatch records and the fire’s early spread. Officials cautioned that descriptions circulated during the investigation were leads, not proof that any particular person had started the fire.

### Reward increased to $250,000

As the investigation widened, government agencies and community organizations combined resources to offer a **$250,000 reward** for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the person or people responsible.

Officials said the unusually large amount reflected the seriousness of the crime and the danger created by setting a fire during extreme wind and drought conditions. An intentionally set brush fire under those circumstances could expose a suspect to charges far more serious than ordinary property damage, particularly if firefighters or residents were killed or injured.

Authorities urged tipsters to provide firsthand information rather than rumors. Useful evidence could include:

- A vehicle parked or moving slowly near the origin area  
- A person seen leaving the roadside shortly before smoke appeared  
- Photographs, cellphone video or dashboard-camera footage  
- Statements by someone claiming responsibility  
- Fuel containers, matches, incendiary devices or other discarded material  
- Information showing that a suspect had knowledge of the ignition before it became public  

The reward did not mean that investigators had identified a suspect. It was intended to break through the limited number of witnesses in the sparsely populated canyon and encourage someone with direct knowledge to come forward.

### Arson arrests elsewhere caused confusion

During the same wildfire emergency, police and fire agencies announced several arson-related arrests in **Los Angeles, San Bernardino, Riverside and other Southern California counties**. The arrests attracted intense attention because they occurred while major fires were burning, but authorities repeatedly stressed that the cases were generally separate.

Some suspects were accused of starting small roadside, brush or vegetation fires that firefighters extinguished before they could grow. Others were detained after witnesses reported seeing them ignite debris or act suspiciously near burned areas. In certain cases, investigators examined whether mental illness, intoxication or reckless behavior played a role.

The arrests did **not** establish that Southern California’s major fires were part of a coordinated arson campaign. Nor did an arson arrest in one county connect a suspect to the Santiago Fire. Each blaze had to be investigated independently through origin analysis, witness testimony, physical evidence and, where available, surveillance footage.

Officials also warned against assuming that every wildfire was intentionally set. During the 2007 outbreak, causes varied. Some fires were investigated as possible arson, while others were associated with power equipment, accidental human activity or remained undetermined.

### No immediate resolution in the Santiago case

Despite the reward, extensive publicity and thousands of investigative hours, authorities did not quickly announce an arrest in the Santiago Fire case. The canyon’s remote terrain, the destruction of evidence by the fire itself and the absence of a clearly identified eyewitness made the investigation difficult.

The distinction between the Santiago inquiry and the other arrests remained central: police were making arson arrests around the region, but none of those announcements by itself solved the Orange County fire.

For residents returning to blackened neighborhoods, the criminal investigation added anger to the losses caused by the flames. Officials said the case would remain open and that the **$250,000 reward** was designed to reach anyone who had withheld information out of fear, loyalty or uncertainty.

The broader wildfire emergency underscored a recurring challenge for Southern California authorities: during periods of extreme fire danger, even a small intentionally set blaze can become a mass-casualty event within minutes. Investigators therefore treated each suspicious ignition as a serious crime while resisting speculation that unrelated suspects or fires were connected without supporting evidence.
